hops.afterHeading: Two questions for any sensory cell
hops.title: Vampire bats retune a pain channel to find warm prey
hops.text: Common vampire bats find warm spots on their prey with infrared-sensing nerve fibres that serve pit organs on the face. Evidence points to TRPV1, which in human sensory neurons responds to painful heat. In the ganglia serving the bat's face, alternative splicing slips a stop codon into the transcript, and roughly two in five TRPV1 transcripts there encode a channel with a shorter tail. Tested alone in lab cells, the short form switched on near 30 degrees C and the full-length form near 40; in body-serving ganglia, over 97 percent of TRPV1 transcripts are full-length. No enzyme sits between heat and pore, so editing the channel retunes the sense.

sources.citation: Gracheva EO et al. Ganglion-specific splicing of TRPV1 underlies infrared sensation in vampire bats. Nature 476:88-91 (2011)

hops.afterHeading: Where a cascade's gain comes from, and what it costs
hops.title: Total darkness does not silence your rods
hops.text: You might assume that in a sealed, pitch-black room your rods go quiet. They do not. Now and then heat alone flips a rhodopsin molecule, and the rod produces an electrical blip that looks just like its response to one real photon. The cascade amplifies the false alarm as faithfully as a real one. Across species, fewer estimated false alarms went with lower light thresholds, though later frog experiments showed shorter signal summation and lower flash sensitivity also mattered. The weakest flash a person reliably detects produces about 10 to 20 rhodopsin isomerizations; one long-standing idea is that this noise is why we cannot reliably see a single photon.

hops.afterHeading: The checklist for calling something the transducer
hops.title: The mustard-oil channel once proposed as the hearing channel
hops.text: In 2004, David Corey's lab, the same Corey as the forty-microsecond study, proposed TRPA1 as a candidate for the hair cell's transduction channel. It passed place and time: its mRNA appeared just as hair cells became mechanosensitive, antibodies labelled the bundles, and blocking its expression reduced hair-cell responses in zebrafish and mice. Then came the loss test. In 2006 two groups, one of them Corey's own, deleted Trpa1 in mice. The mice startled normally to loud noise, kept their balance, and had normal hearing responses and vestibular hair-cell currents. Instead, their pain responses to mustard oil were weakened or lost, depending on the test.

audio.title: Vampire bats, slow toads and salty licorice
audio.transcript:
What sits between a stimulus and the pore? Three stories from three very different animals.

Start with one heat-sensing channel, T R P V one, and a detour through chili peppers. In most mammals, T R P V one opens for painful heat and for capsaicin, the burning compound in chilies. Birds are indifferent to capsaicin's burn. In lab tests, heat and acid opened the chicken version of T R P V one, which is much less sensitive to capsaicin than the mammalian channel. So birds eat the fruit and spread the seeds.

Common vampire bats push the same channel in another direction. In sampled dorsal root ganglia serving the body, the full-length transcript predominates, encoding a channel whose heat threshold in lab cells sits near forty degrees Celsius. But in the trigeminal ganglia serving the pit organs on the face, different splicing slips a stop codon into the transcript, and a large share of the T R P V one transcripts there encode the shorter form. Tested on its own in lab cells, that short version started opening at about thirty degrees Celsius, roughly ten degrees below the full-length form. That lower threshold could help explain how the bats pick out warm spots on prey. No enzyme sits in between, so change the channel and you change the sense.

Now the other design, an enzyme cascade, as in a rod. Passing one photon's signal through rhodopsin and its enzyme partners buys extraordinary sensitivity in dim light. But the cascade also multiplies the rare moments when heat alone flips a rhodopsin molecule, false alarms that look identical to single photons. Those false alarms come more often at higher temperatures, so a cool toad retina has an edge against this kind of noise. At about sixteen degrees Celsius, some common toads will snap at a moving dummy worm so faint that it delivers only one photoisomerization per fifty rods per second.

Here is the catch. To pull that tiny signal out of the dark, the toad's retinal output cells add up light over a long window, and near threshold they take around three seconds to respond. The picture reaching the brain shows the worm where it was seconds earlier. As the light dimmed, the snaps landed further and further toward the rear of the dummy, and finally missed it. Oddly, right at threshold the toads aimed better than that delay predicts, as if the brain were correcting for its own slow vision.

Last, a question this lesson keeps asking: how do you prove a protein is the transducer? Think of salty licorice, a candy popular in Scandinavia with a distinctive, acquired taste. It has ammonium chloride added. In twenty twenty-three, researchers showed that ammonium chloride activates O T O P one, the proton channel that type three taste cells use to sense sour. For sufficiency, cultured cells given human, mouse, chicken or zebrafish O T O P one gained a large inward current in response to ammonium chloride, and in cells expressing mouse O T O P one, p H measurements showed their insides growing more alkaline alongside the current. For a clue to how it works, changing one conserved arginine on the inside of the mouse channel cut the ammonium chloride response relative to the acid response. And for loss, isolated type three taste cells from mice lacking O T O P one stopped firing in response to ammonium chloride, and the taste nerve's response was strongly reduced.

In each story, the first steps of transduction decide which stimuli make a signal at all. And in the toad, what the retina does next trades speed for sensitivity.
